props.title: The Kids Are Alright
props.initialSlug: The Who documentary spanning their career

sections.content: The Kids Are Alright (1979) stands as the definitive documentary of The Who at their peak, capturing the raw energy and destruction that made them legendary. Director Jeff Stein assembles rare footage spanning 1964-1978, including their explosive appearances on The Smothers Brothers Show where Keith Moon's drum kit actually exploded. The film contrasts dramatically with sanitized rock docs like Let It Be (1970), instead embracing the band's chaos and letting their personalities shine through unfiltered interviews. Pete Townshend's guitar-smashing, Roger Daltrey's microphone-swinging, and Moon's manic drumming create a portrait of rock at its most visceral.

sections.content: The late 1970s marked a golden age for rock documentaries, with filmmakers moving beyond simple concert footage to explore the personalities and conflicts behind the music. The Last Waltz (1978) brought unprecedented cinematographic sophistication to the genre, while Monterey Pop (1968) captured the moment rock became a cultural force. The Kids Are Alright distinguished itself by incorporating television appearances, interviews, and rare footage to create a comprehensive band biography that influenced countless music documentaries that followed. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Music Documentary Filmmaking

The film's influence can be seen in later works like Some Kind of Monster (2004), which similarly exposed band tensions and personalities, and It Might Get Loud (2008), which explored guitar heroes with the same reverence for musical craftsmanship. Director Jeff Stein's approach to archival footage and his willingness to show both triumphs and disasters created a template for honest music storytelling that continues in films like Amy (2015) and Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck (2015).
